passage:
Sunday night
Lavanya laughed at me this morning: three video calls before breakfast. Nani's weekly one, Khala asking about her son's college forms, and my cousin Imtiaz showing off his new puppy. I don't mind. Nobody lives in the same lane anymore; we're spread over four cities, so if I don't call, the thread just slips. Last month I took two days' leave when Chhoti Khala was in hospital and slept on the bench beside her bed. Next week is Eid, and the train ticket home is already booked. Living alone here is my choice. Staying close is also my choice, just one I have to keep making.
Rehana

qa.q: How many video calls did Rehana make before breakfast?
qa.a: Three video calls.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel about the effort of keeping in touch?
qa.a: Rehana feels content and committed rather than burdened; the calls are a chosen way to stay close to a family spread over four cities.

qa.q: Which of Rehana's habits keep the family close, and why?
qa.a: Regular calls, turning up in person when Chhoti Khala needed help, and going home for Eid, because closeness now depends on effort, not a shared lane.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see Rehana's morning of calls?
qa.a: Lavanya may find it funny or tiring at first, but might also admire how much Rehana cares for relatives who live far away.

grounding: Shows a young adult living separately who keeps close ties with the extended family through calls, festivals and practical support, treating closeness as a choice kept by effort.

Arohi: Dadi asked why you didn't come for Ganpati this year 😔
Disha: I know. Work launch, no leave. I video called during the aarti though!
Arohi: She saw. She held the phone up to the idol the whole time 😄
Disha: Tell her I'm coming for Diwali. Four days, ticket booked.
Arohi: She'll count them. Also Kaka's shop is shifting next Saturday, lots of lifting.
Disha: I'll take the early bus Saturday and help, back Sunday night.
Arohi: You'd do that?
Disha: Obviously. Living in Pune doesn't mean I left.
Arohi: Dadi says the house feels smaller without you.
Disha: Tell her that's why I call every Wednesday. She's my favourite person to annoy 🙂

qa.q: How many days is Disha coming home for Diwali?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What does Disha's quick offer to help with the shop suggest about Disha's feelings for the family?
qa.a: It suggests Disha feels loyal and loving towards the family and still belongs there, even while living in Pune.

qa.q: Which of Disha's habits keep the tie strong across the distance?
qa.a: Wednesday calls, joining the aarti by video, booking Diwali early and turning up to help Kaka shift the shop.

qa.q: How does Dadi seem to experience Disha living away?
qa.a: Dadi misses Disha and says the house feels smaller, but holding the phone up during the aarti shows the calls still let her feel close.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult living apart who keeps close ties with the extended family through calls, festivals and practical help, showing closeness kept by effort rather than a shared address.

passage:
Every second Saturday, Jomon took the early bus from Kochi to the family's old house outside Kottayam, a bag of bakery rusks for Ammachi in his hand. He had lived in his own rented room near the port for two years now, and the village didn't let him forget it.

"Ah, the city boy visits," an uncle teased.

But it was Jomon who had set up the Sunday video call for the cousins in the Gulf, Jomon who drove Ammachi to her eye check-ups, and Jomon who, this Onam, split the sadya cooking into a list so Vandana chechi wasn't stuck in the kitchen alone.

At night on the verandah, Vandana handed him a banana chip. "You live the farthest of all of us still in Kerala," she said, "and you're the one who shows up."

Jomon shrugged. "Showing up is the easy part. I just put it in my calendar."

qa.q: What does Jomon bring for Ammachi?
qa.a: Jomon brings a bag of bakery rusks for Ammachi.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when an uncle calls him 'the city boy'?
qa.a: He may feel a small sting at being seen as the one who left, though he takes it lightly and keeps showing up.

qa.q: Which of Jomon's habits keep the family close?
qa.a: Fortnightly visits, the cousins' Sunday video call, driving Ammachi and dividing the Onam cooking; he keeps closeness by planned effort.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Jomon's effort?
qa.a: Vandana is grateful: though he lives farthest, he is the one who shows up and makes sure she isn't alone in the kitchen.

grounding: Shows a young adult who lives separately but keeps close ties through visits, calls, festivals and practical help.

passage:
At six in the morning in Prague it was lunchtime in Chengdu, and Xin's grandmother was turning eighty.

Xin couldn't fly home this year. So for a month she had been quietly organising: each of the eleven cousins recorded a short message, and Xin stitched them into one video. She had posted a scarf in March so it would arrive in time.

Now she stood in the tiny flat kitchen with her flatmate Jana, stirring long-life noodles for the call.

"Why noodles at six a.m.?" Jana yawned.

"So we eat together," Xin said, propping the phone against the kettle.

On the screen her grandmother held up the scarf, then watched the video and cried. The whole table in Chengdu raised their bowls to the camera. In Prague, Xin and Jana raised theirs back.

qa.q: How many cousins recorded messages?
qa.a: Each of the eleven cousins recorded a short message.

qa.q: What does Xin's month of quiet organising suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: Xin feels homesick for the family table and cares enough to plan closeness carefully rather than leave it to chance.

qa.q: What made Xin's long-distance closeness work?
qa.a: She planned ahead, posting the scarf in March and gathering the video, and timed a shared meal so the family could eat together across the distance.

qa.q: What is the early-morning noodle pot like for Jana?
qa.a: Jana is sleepy and puzzled at first, but gets drawn into the family meal, raising a bowl alongside Xin.

grounding: Shows a young adult living abroad who keeps close family ties by effort, planning a shared birthday meal across the distance.

passage:
At lunch in the Hyderabad office cafeteria, Kamal found Nikita bent over a spreadsheet that had nothing to do with work.

"Quarterly numbers?"

"My cousin's wedding in Warangal," she said. "Forty relatives, three buses, one list."

Kamal laughed. "I thought you moved here to get away from all that."

"I moved here for the job and a room of my own." She highlighted a row. "I didn't move away from them. I call Nani every evening at eight, I go home the last weekend of every month, and when Chinni's wedding came up, I said I'd handle the transport."

"That's a lot."

"It's what living alone and still being family takes. I'd rather do it than lose them."

At 1:30 sharp she logged back into work, the bus list saved in the next tab.

qa.q: How many relatives are on Nikita's list?
qa.a: Forty relatives, three buses, one list.

qa.q: What does Nikita's answer to Kamal suggest about how she feels about her family?
qa.a: She feels deeply attached and a little proud; she chose a room of her own but values them enough to call, visit and organise.

qa.q: What habits help Nikita balance both worlds?
qa.a: A fixed eight o'clock call to Nani, a monthly weekend at home, and taking on concrete tasks like the wedding transport in her own time.

qa.q: How does Kamal see Nikita's move to Hyderabad at first?
qa.a: Kamal assumed she moved to get away from family, and is surprised by how much effort she puts into staying close.

grounding: Shows a young adult living separately who keeps close ties with the wider family through daily calls, monthly visits and practical help.

passage:
Dear Tejas,
You asked how I manage to still feel close to everyone since moving to Bengaluru. Honestly, it takes work, and I like the work.
Every Sunday at eleven I call Aaji, even if it's just to hear her complain about the maid. I'm in the cousins' group and I actually reply, not just hearts. When your mother had her surgery, I flew up for two days and sat with her while you were at your exams. For Ganpati, I take leave. For Diwali, I send small boxes to each house with a note, because Aaji says that's what her mother did.
Some relatives think I've "left the family" because I don't live in the big Nashik house. But I think we're closer than when I lived there and we fought about bathroom time.
Call me when you're in the city. You can stay.
Your didi, Shreya

qa.q: What time does Shreya call Aaji every Sunday?
qa.a: At eleven.

qa.q: How does Shreya feel about the effort of staying close?
qa.a: She feels warm and committed, saying it takes work and she likes the work.

qa.q: Which of Shreya's habits keep the family close, and why?
qa.a: Weekly calls, replying in the cousins' group, taking leave for festivals and showing up for surgery; regular effort keeps bonds alive without living together.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel about his didi after his mother's surgery?
qa.a: Tejas probably feels grateful and close to Shreya, who sat with his mother while he took his exams.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult who keeps close ties with extended family by calls, festivals and support while living separately.
